transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you. Could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Nice to meet you too. Well, I guess... I'm here because I just cannot seem to keep my work in order anymore. I work at a laundry and dry cleaning place, and, you know, it's a busy job, there's always people coming in and out, but lately it's just become this huge, unmanageable mess. 

I've got the customer claim tickets, the credit card receipts, all my little handwritten workshop notes about, you know, which shirt needs heavy starch or which dress has a grease stain that needs special spotting... and then the actual customer jobs themselves, the garments in the bags, it's all just piled together. Just these big, overwhelming piles everywhere on the front counter and in the back room. 

And I'll just stand there staring at it, and I honestly do not know what to handle first. It used to be that I could sort of manage it, maybe make little separate stacks or use paperclips, but now the receipts get mixed right in with the workshop notes, and then a customer walks in the door and I'm just frantically digging through this absolute mountain of paper trying to figure out what's what. It's just so frustrating because I want to do a good job, I've been doing this kind of work for a long time, but I look at the piles now and I just freeze up. I literally have no idea where to even start with it all anymore.
Has this difficulty with organizing your work and feeling overwhelmed always been a struggle for you, or is this something that has only started happening more recently?

Well, you know, looking back... it's a really good question, because I guess I've always been a little bit on the messy side, maybe, but not like this. Not this bad, where it's actually stopping me from doing my job. The real trouble, the part where I'm just completely paralyzed by the piles and the receipts, that really started about... oh, I'd say exactly two years and two months ago. I know the timeline pretty well because of what was happening at the shop right then. 

See, that was right when I decided—and honestly, I thought it was a brilliant idea at the time—to start changing the business into this much more complicated boutique model. You know, instead of just your standard wash-and-fold or basic dry cleaning, I wanted to offer specialized care. Like hand-pressing vintage linens, organic solvent options for delicate silks, custom spot-treatments... really high-end, personalized service. I spent months thinking about it, figuring it would bring in better clientele, and it did! It really did. But oh my goodness, the details! 

Every single item suddenly needed a custom tag, and special instructions, and different processing times. Before, it was just "in on Tuesday, out on Thursday," you know? But with the boutique model, Mrs. Higgins' silk blouse needs a three-day turnaround with a specific eco-friendly spot treatment, and then Mr. Peterson's wool suit needs the standard press but with a rush fee, and my old way of doing things just completely fell apart. I thought I could just adapt, just write more notes and use more paperclips, but it's been two years and a couple of months of just absolute chaos since I made that switch. I just didn't anticipate how many moving parts would come with upgrading the business, and now every time I try to sort it out, I just get so overwhelmed thinking about how simple it used to be. I just wanted to make the shop nicer, you know, but the complication of it all is just... it's just too much.
Over the past two years, have you noticed any persistent changes in your appetite, your sleep, or your energy levels?

No, not really. I mean, my appetite is pretty much the same as it's always been. I still eat my regular meals, you know, maybe grab a sandwich from the deli next door to the shop for lunch, or bring some leftovers. I haven't noticed myself eating way more or way less, or suddenly craving weird things, or losing my taste for food. It's just... normal. And my sleep is fine too. I usually get to bed around the same time, maybe watch a little TV to unwind after dealing with all those piles at work, but once my head hits the pillow, I'm out. I sleep straight through the night and wake up when my alarm goes off. I don't toss and turn, and I don't wake up at three in the morning worrying about the dry cleaning, which is a blessing, honestly, because I worry enough about it during the day! 

And as for my energy, well, I feel like I have the same amount of energy I've always had. I'm up and moving around the shop all day, carrying bags of clothes, running the press, dealing with customers. I don't feel physically exhausted or drained, like I need a nap in the middle of the afternoon. It's not my body that's tired, you know? It's just my brain that feels completely stuck when I look at all that paperwork and the special instructions. But physically? My energy, my sleep, my eating... all of that is perfectly fine. It's just the organizing and the overwhelming mess that's the problem.
Do you find that you feel anxious or worried about many other things in your life outside of the issues you're having at the shop?

Well, no, not really. I mean, it's funny you ask that, because my sister, she's a worrier, you know? She worries about the news, she worries about the weather, she worries if her kids are eating enough vegetables—which they are, they're grown adults, but she still worries. But me? No. Outside of the shop, I'm actually pretty easygoing. 

I don't sit around fretting about my health, or the bills at home, or, I don't know, the roof leaking or anything like that. My house is actually pretty peaceful. I have a little garden in the back, just some tomatoes and a few marigolds, nothing fancy, but I go out there on Sunday mornings and I don't feel anxious at all. I just water the plants and listen to the birds. It's really just the shop. 

And it's not even a general worry about the shop, like "Oh no, what if we go out of business?" It's literally just that moment, that specific feeling when I walk in and see the counter, and there's Mrs. Higgins' eco-friendly slip lying on top of a pile of standard wash-and-fold receipts, and a bag of dry cleaning that needs a special spot treatment just leaning against the register, and I think, "How am I going to get through this?" That's when I get that tight feeling. But the rest of my life? No, I don't really have that kind of general anxiety or worry about other things. It's really just those piles and all those complicated new instructions that I brought on myself.
Looking back at your childhood and your time in school, did you frequently struggle with staying organized, finishing tasks, or keeping track of your belongings back then?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about that, because I was actually just talking to my sister about this the other day. We were going through some old boxes in the attic—well, she was going through them, I was mostly just looking at things and getting distracted by old photos—but she found this stack of my old report cards from elementary school. And oh boy, reading those was like looking in a mirror, honestly. 

Even way back then, in grade school, it was always the same story. Every single teacher, from Mrs. Gable in second grade to Mr. Henderson in fifth, they all wrote the exact same thing to my mother. They'd say, "She's a very bright girl, very capable," but then would come the "but." It was always, "but she's so scattered." And it was true! I mean, I would have my homework done, maybe, but could I find it in my desk? Absolutely not. My desk was like a black hole for assignments, permission slips, you name it. I was constantly losing papers. I'd shove them in a textbook, or they'd get crumpled at the bottom of my backpack, and then when it was time to turn them in, I'd be digging around frantically while everyone else was already moving on to the next thing.

And it wasn't just the organizing, either. The teachers were always telling my mom that I was talking out of turn. I just couldn't seem to hold a thought in—if something popped into my head, I had to say it right then and there, even if Mrs. Gable was in the middle of a math lesson. I'd just blurt it out. And finishing things? Oh, forget about it. I'd start a project with all this enthusiasm, coloring the title page perfectly, and then halfway through, I'd just drift off or start looking out the window, and they'd have to come tap on my desk and remind me, over and over, to actually finish the work. So, yeah, I guess that feeling of being a bit all over the place, losing track of things and needing a push to get to the finish line... that's been there since I was a little girl in pigtails, long before I ever thought about running a dry cleaning business.
